lines.text: Vera, what changes when a model uses a tool?
Nothing. It still predicts tokens; tools are just text in context.
Then who runs them?
Your code. The model writes a strict-format call; your code runs it and appends the result.
Then it predicts again, until done. That loop is an agent.
Show me a real one.
The guide's run: find the top complaint, draft a reply.
Each result joins the context; every model call re-reads all of it.
Heavier every step?
Over 5,000 tokens. Caching the repeated start saves 47%.
lines.say: Over five thousand tokens. Caching the repeated start saves forty-seven percent.

lines.text: Then it stops until a human approves the reply.
Why not give agents every job?
Errors compound: 95% per step over 20 steps is about 36%.
lines.say: Errors compound: ninety-five percent per step over twenty steps is about thirty-six percent.

lines.text: So agents need self-checks, retries, and tools that fail loudly.
With fixed steps, a simple workflow is cheaper and easier to test.
Agents for open-ended jobs, then.
What if a web page gives my agent orders?
That's prompt injection. Tool results are untrusted input.
Defend by design: least privilege per tool, text as data, log every call.
And a human approves anything irreversible: sending, paying, deleting, deploying.
Even tools plugged in through MCP?
lines.say: Even tools plugged in through M C P?

lines.text: Same rules. MCP is a standard plug, not a trust badge.
lines.say: Same rules. M C P is a standard plug, not a trust badge.

lines.text: Can I run one myself?
Step through the agent run and drag the reliability sliders in the Agents chapter.
One loop at a time, a human at the gate.
